mainTopic: Oaths for those suspected about money, and grabbing the disputed garment in front of בית דין
overview: The amud opens by testing whether someone suspected about money is also suspected of swearing falsely (מיגו דחשיד אממונא חשיד אשבועתא). Rulings of רב נחמן, רבי חייא and רב ששת all make such a person swear, so the גמרא concludes that we do not say this. אביי pushes back: in those cases the person may only be unsure about an old loan, so he is not a real thief. רב ששת בריה דרב אידי explains why the oath still helps: people grab doubtful money because it can be returned, but they fear a doubtful oath because it can never be undone. Then רבי זירא asks what happens if one of the two people holding the טלית grabs it in front of בית דין, specifically when the other was silent at first and protested later. רב נחמן tries to prove the answer from a ברייתא, but the גמרא pushes the proof away in two ways. The גמרא then asks how this question affects making the garment הקדש without grabbing it, weighing the power of words to הקדש against the rule that one can only make holy what is in his possession. A story that may answer this begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Challenge from רב נחמן's oath of inducement
steps.stepSummary: If a money-suspect can't swear, how can רב נחמן require a שבועת היסת from someone who denies a whole claim?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then what about רב נחמן's ruling that we make him swear a שבועת היסת? Let us say: since he is suspected about money, he is suspected about the oath too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that someone suspected about money cannot be given an oath. It points to רב נחמן, who does make such a person swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן says that a person who denies an entire claim must swear a שבועת היסת. בית דין only makes him swear because they suspect he might really owe the money. If being suspected about money meant he was also suspected of lying under oath, the oath would be pointless, yet רב נחמן still requires it.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath of inducement, a rabbinic oath imposed on someone who denies a claim entirely
Since; here meaning 'since this is true, that is also true'

phrases.english: But then, that which Rav Nachman said:
we make him swear an oath of inducement,
phrases.notes: This is said about someone who denies the whole claim against him, saying he owes nothing at all.

phrases.english: let us say: since he is suspected regarding money,
he is suspected regarding an oath!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא הָא דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier assumption that a money-suspect cannot be given an oath.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption מיגו דחשיד אממונא חשיד אשבועתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב נחמן imposes an oath precisely on someone suspected of denying a real debt; if such suspicion disqualified oaths, his ruling could not stand.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי חייא's storekeeper and worker case
steps.stepSummary: In רבי חייא's ברייתא both sides swear and collect from the employer, even though one of them must be lying.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, what about the ברייתא of רבי חייא: both of them swear and collect from the employer? Let us say: since he is suspected about money, he is suspected about the oath!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ruling that seems to contradict the idea. In רבי חייא's ברייתא, two people whose claims cannot both be true are each allowed to swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The storekeeper and the worker each claim the employer's money, and one of them must be making a false claim. Even so, רבי חייא lets both of them swear and collect. If a money-suspect were automatically suspected of swearing falsely, the oath would not be allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: And furthermore; introduces an additional challenge

phrases.english: And furthermore, that which Rabbi Chiya taught:
both of them swear and collect from the employer,
phrases.notes: These are the storekeeper and the worker from earlier, on דף ג, who both claim payment from the same employer.

phrases.english: let us say: since he is suspected regarding money,
he is suspected regarding an oath!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתוּ הָא דְתָנֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second challenge against the same assumption.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption מיגו דחשיד אממונא חשיד אשבועתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One of the two people must be claiming money falsely, yet both are allowed to swear.

steps.title: Challenge from רב ששת's three oaths for a שומר
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת makes a שומר swear three oaths, even though those oaths exist only because we suspect him about money.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, רב ששת said we make him swear three oaths: that I was not negligent with it, that I did not take it for my own use, and that it is not in my possession. Let us say: since he is suspected about money, he is suspected about the oath!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third ruling. רב ששת has a שומר swear three separate oaths, each answering a suspicion about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each oath answers a specific suspicion: that he was careless, that he used the item for himself, or that he still has it. בית דין plainly suspects him about money, yet they still trust his oath. This again contradicts the idea that money-suspicion rules out an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: I misused it; I took it for my own use

phrases.english: And furthermore, that which Rav Sheshet said:
we make him swear three oaths:
phrases.notes: This is about an unpaid watchman who claims the item he was guarding was stolen.

phrases.english: an oath that I was not negligent with it,
an oath that I did not take it for my own use,
an oath that it is not in my possession.
Let us say: since he is suspected regarding money,
he is suspected regarding an oath!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתוּ הָא דְּאָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third challenge against the same assumption.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption מיגו דחשיד אממונא חשיד אשבועתא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The third oath, that it is not in his possession, exists only because we suspect he kept the item, yet we trust him to swear.

steps.title: Conclusion: suspicion about money does not cancel an oath
steps.stepSummary: Because of these three rulings, the גמרא concludes that we do not say מיגו דחשיד אממונא חשיד אשבועתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we do not say that since he is suspected about money, he is suspected about an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws its conclusion from the three challenges. Being suspected about money does not automatically make someone suspected of swearing falsely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three rulings require an oath from someone we suspect about money, so the original assumption cannot be right. A person may be tempted to grab money and still not be willing to swear a false oath, which is much more serious. That is why בית דין can rely on his שבועה.
steps.whatToRemember: The three rulings of רב נחמן, רבי חייא, and רב ששת lead the גמרא to say we do NOT say מיגו דחשיד אממונא חשיד אשבועתא. But this is not the last word: in the next step אביי explains these same cases another way, so they no longer prove the rule.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't confuse this מיגו with the familiar מיגו that strengthens a claim ("he could have made a better claim"). Here מיגו just means "since": since he is suspect about one thing, is he suspect about another?

phrases.english: Rather, we do not say
that since he is suspected regarding money,
he is suspected regarding an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָא אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion forced by the three preceding challenges.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: We do not say מיגו דחשיד אממונא חשיד אשבועתא; a person suspected about money may still take an oath.

steps.title: אביי: maybe he thinks he is owed an old loan
steps.stepSummary: אביי rejects the proof from the three rulings. Maybe the person keeps the money because he believes the other side owes him from an old loan, so he is not a real thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: We worry that maybe he has an old loan owed to him by the other person.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי pushes back on the conclusion of step 4. He says the three rulings don't prove anything, because the person in those cases might not be a true money-thief.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof assumed the defendant is suspected of plain stealing, and yet we still let him swear. אביי says no: he may be holding the money as payback for a מלוה ישנה he thinks is owed to him. Someone like that is not a real thief, so these cases tell us nothing about a true חשיד אממונא.

keyTerms.meaning: we are concerned / we worry about the possibility
he has a claim against him (the other person owes him)

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not saying the defendant really is owed money. He is only offering another way to read the three cases, so they no longer prove the rule.

phrases.english: Abaye said: We are concerned

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמָּא מִלְוֶה יְשָׁנָה יֵשׁ לוֹ עָלָיו.
phrases.english: that perhaps he has an old loan owed to him by the other person.
phrases.notes: "He" is the one denying the claim; he may feel he's just collecting what's his.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּיֵי אָמַר: חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא מִלְוֶה יְשָׁנָה יֵשׁ לוֹ עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof that led to the conclusion in step 4
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from all three rulings (רב נחמן, רבי חייא, רב ששת)
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the defendant is a real thief. He may instead think he is collecting an old debt, so he is not truly חשיד אממונא.

steps.title: Then why make him swear at all?
steps.stepSummary: If he really has an old loan, he is entitled to keep the money. So why should he have to swear?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let him take it without an oath!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי's idea. If the defendant really has an old loan, the oath seems pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the defendant truly has a מלוה ישנה, then keeping the money is his right. In that case the oath decides nothing, and he could simply keep the money with no שבועה. Yet the rulings do require an oath, so אביי's explanation doesn't fit.

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: Meaning: if he really has an old loan coming to him.

phrases.english: let him take it without an oath!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי נִשְׁקוֹל בְּלָא שְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's explanation in step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's suggestion that the defendant has an old loan
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he truly is owed the money, the oath accomplishes nothing. The law should let him keep it without swearing, yet the rulings require an oath.

steps.title: אביי adjusted: he is only unsure about the old loan
steps.stepSummary: אביי's idea is restated. The defendant is not sure he has an old loan, so he holds the money just in case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we worry that maybe he is unsure whether he has an old loan owed to him by the other person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes אביי's idea to answer the challenge. The person is not sure he is owed money; he only suspects it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the oath makes sense. A person who only has a doubt might grab the money, but he would hesitate to swear falsely over a doubt. So the oath can still bring out the truth, and he is still not a real thief.

keyTerms.meaning: a doubtful old loan (he is unsure whether it exists)

phrases.english: Rather, we are concerned that perhaps

phrases.aramaic: סְפֵק מִלְוֶה יְשָׁנָה יֵשׁ לוֹ עָלָיו.
phrases.english: he has a doubtful old loan owed to him by the other person.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא סְפֵק מִלְוֶה יְשָׁנָה יֵשׁ לוֹ עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 by adjusting step 5
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: a certain old loan becomes a doubtful old loan
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The defendant knows for sure he is owed money, so an oath would be pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The defendant only suspects he is owed money. He holds the money just in case, but an oath may stop him, so it serves a purpose.

steps.title: If he grabs money over a doubt, he'll swear over a doubt
steps.stepSummary: Someone willing to take another person's money because of a doubt would also be willing to swear because of that doubt. So how does the oath help?
steps.simpleTranslation: But don't we say: just as he grabs money because of a doubt, he will also swear because of a doubt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the adjusted version of אביי's idea. It argues that a doubt that lets him grab money will also let him swear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 said the defendant would hold the money on a doubt but would not swear on one. The גמרא says these go together. If his doubt is enough for him to seize property, it is enough for him to take an oath, so the oath would not bring out the truth.

phrases.english: But don't we say:
he grabs money because of a doubt?
So he will also swear because of a doubt!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָאו אָמְרִינַן תָּפֵיס מָמוֹנָא מִסְּפֵיקָא מִשְׁתְּבַע נָמֵי מִסָּפֵק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the revised explanation of step 7
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that a person unsure of an old loan will hold money but will not swear
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Grabbing money and swearing should follow the same logic. If a doubt is enough for him to seize, it is enough for him to swear, so the oath is useless.

steps.title: People fear a doubtful oath more than doubtful money
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת בריה דרב אידי answers that people hold back from a doubtful שבועה even when they do not hold back from doubtful money, because money can be returned but an oath cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת, son of רב אידי, said: People hold back from swearing when they are not sure, but they do not hold back from taking money when they are not sure. Why? Money can be given back. An oath cannot be taken back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 8. A person who takes money because of a doubt will still not swear because of that doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 said: if he keeps money out of doubt, he will also swear out of doubt, so the oath is useless. רב ששת answers that the two are not equal in a person's mind. If he turns out to be wrong about the money, he can still return it. A false שבועה can never be undone, so he is more careful with it, and the oath does its job.

keyTerms.meaning: They hold back, they stay away
An oath he is not sure is true
Money he is not sure belongs to him
Cannot be given back or undone

steps.whatToRemember: The oath in our משנה makes sense even for someone who might grab money out of doubt. People take money lightly because it can be returned, but a false שבועה can never be fixed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This saves the reason for the oath in the משנה. אביי's idea, that the holder is only acting out of doubt, no longer makes the שבועה pointless.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi, said:
People hold back from an oath they are unsure about
but they do not hold back from money they are unsure about.
What is the reason?
Money can be returned,
an oath cannot be taken back.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי: פָּרְשִׁי אִינָשֵׁי מִסְּפֵק שְׁבוּעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 8 that someone who grabs money out of doubt would also swear out of doubt.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Psychological distinction: people treat money and oaths differently.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A person who takes money out of doubt will just as easily swear out of doubt, so the oath does nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: People are more careful with oaths because an oath cannot be undone, so the oath still works.

steps.title: One person grabs the garment in front of the judges
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks what the law is if one of the two people holding the טלית grabs it from the other in front of the בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא asked: If one of them seized the garment in front of us, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question begins. רבי זירא asks about the משנה's case of two people holding a טלית, where one grabs the whole thing in front of the judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, both people are holding the garment and they split it. Here one of them pulls it away completely in front of the בית דין. The question is whether that grab changes anything. Does he now count as the only holder, or do we ignore it?

keyTerms.meaning: He asks, he raises a question he cannot yet answer
He seized it, he grabbed it by force
In front of us, in front of the judges

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira asked:
If one seized it in our presence, what is the law?
phrases.notes: "It" is the garment from the משנה that both people were holding.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַבִּי זֵירָא: תְּקָפָהּ אֶחָד בְּפָנֵינוּ, מַהוּ?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the oath discussion is resolved.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does grabbing the garment in front of the בית דין change who is treated as holding it?

steps.title: How can this case be a real question?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי זירא's question. If the other person stayed silent, he admitted. If he protested, he did all he could. Either way the answer seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the other person stayed quiet, he admitted to him. And if he shouted, what more could he have done?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what case רבי זירא could mean, because both options seem to have a clear answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the person whose garment was grabbed said nothing, his silence shows he agrees the other one owns it. If he shouted in protest, that is all he can do, and the grab should not help the stronger person. So there seems to be no real doubt in either case.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What does it look like?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If he was silent, he has admitted to him.
phrases.notes: "He" is the person the garment was taken from. Saying nothing looks like agreeing.

phrases.english: And if he shouted,
what should he have done?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִי דְּשָׁתֵיק, אוֹדוֹיֵי אוֹדִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רבי זירא's question in Step 10 has any real case behind it.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי זירא's question about the grab in front of the judges.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both possible cases have obvious answers. Silence means he admitted, and shouting means he protested as much as he could. So there is nothing to ask.

steps.title: The case: silent at first, protesting later
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the question is about a person who was silent at first and only shouted later.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the question is needed where he was silent at first and then shouted. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 11 by naming a mixed case that really is in doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 only looked at a person who was always silent or always shouting. Here he did both: silent first, then protesting. Now it is not clear which reaction counts.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for this case

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where he was silent at first and later shouted. What is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא דִּשְׁתֵיק מֵעִיקָּרָא וַהֲדַר צָוַוח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 11 by naming a case that is truly unclear.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a mixed situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The person was either always silent or always shouting, so the answer is obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question is about someone who was silent first and shouted afterward.

steps.title: Was the silence an admission, or did he trust the judges?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא lays out both sides. Either his first silence was an admission, or his later shouting shows he was quiet only because he thought the judges had seen the grab.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he was silent, did he admit to him? Or maybe, since he is shouting now, it becomes clear why he was quiet at first. He thought: the judges are watching him, so I do not need to say anything.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the two ways to look at the case from Step 12. The next steps try to answer it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: silence at the moment of the grab is an admission, and the later shouting is just regret. Side two: the later shouting shows what he meant all along. He stayed quiet only because he assumed the רבנן of the בית דין saw what happened and would protect him.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter has been revealed, it becomes clear

steps.confusionAlert: "Rabbis" here does not mean famous sages in general. It means the judges of the בית דין who saw the grab happen.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי זירא's question is about silence followed by protest. Does the first silence count as agreeing, or does the later protest show the silence only meant 'the judges already saw'?

phrases.english: Since he was silent, he admitted to him,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא: כֵּיוָן דְּקָא צָוַוח הַשְׁתָּא
phrases.english: or perhaps, since he is shouting now,
it is revealed that the reason he was silent at first

phrases.aramaic: סָבַר: הָא קָא חָזוּ לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן.
phrases.english: is that he thought: the Rabbis are seeing him.
phrases.notes: The judges are watching the grab, so he felt no need to protest right away.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדְּאִשְׁתִּיק אוֹדוֹיֵי אוֹדִי לֵיהּ, אוֹ דִלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains both sides of the question in the case defined in Step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do we judge him by his first silence (admission) or by his later protest (he was silent only because the judges were watching)?

steps.title: רב נחמן quotes a teaching about who must bring proof
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן quotes a ברייתא. Both people swear and split the garment only when both are holding it. If only one is holding it, the other must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: Come and hear. When is this rule said? When both of them are holding the garment. But if the garment was in the hand of only one of them, the one who wants to take it from his friend must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן brings a ברייתא to try to answer רבי זירא's question. This step only quotes the source. The next step explains how it proves anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא limits the משנה's rule of swearing and splitting to a case where both people hold the טלית. If only one holds it, he keeps it unless the other brings proof.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case are these words said? It limits an earlier rule
The one who wants to take from his friend must bring proof

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: Come and hear:
In what case are these words said?
When both of them are holding onto it,
but if the garment was coming out
from under the hand of one of them,
the one who takes from his friend must bring the proof.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב נחמן תא שמע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question laid out in step 13
steps.raayaObject: רבי זירא's question about grabbing the טלית in front of the בית דין
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about one person holding the garment

steps.title: The teaching must be about a grab in front of the court
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא cannot simply mean one person was holding the garment, because that would be obvious. So it must mean one person grabbed it in front of the court, and he keeps it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If we say it means just what it says, that is obvious! Rather, it must be where one of them grabbed it in front of us.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רב נחמן's ברייתא proves something. Its plain meaning is too obvious, so it must be talking about רבי זירא's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone knows that a person who holds something keeps it unless the other side brings proof. A ברייתא would not bother teaching that. So it must be teaching something new: even a person who grabbed the garment in front of the בית דין keeps it.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the details?
In front of us, meaning in front of the court

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a common move in the גמרא: if a source's plain meaning is too obvious, it must be teaching something new.

phrases.english: What is the case?
If we say it is as it is taught, that is obvious!
Rather, it is where one grabbed it in front of us.

steps.triggerLanguage: היכי דמי אי נימא כדקתני פשיטא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the ברייתא from step 14 proves the point
steps.raayaObject: That a person who grabs the garment in front of the בית דין keeps it
steps.raayaSupportSource: The plain reading of the ברייתא is too obvious, so it must mean this case

steps.title: The teaching may be about a claim that the other side admitted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers a different case. They were told to split the garment and later came back with one holding it. He says the other admitted it was his, and the other says he only rented it to him. The renter claim is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Here we are dealing with a case where they came before us while both were holding it, and we told them, "Go split it." They left, and then came back with only one of them holding it. This one says, "He admitted to me." That one says, "I rented it to him for money." We say to him: "Until now you suspected him of being a robber, and now you rent it to him without witnesses?"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away רב נחמן's proof. It explains the ברייתא as talking about a different case, not a grab in front of the court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the holder did not grab the garment in front of the court. He got it outside, and he says the other person admitted it was his. The claim "I rented it to him" does not make sense, because nobody rents something to a person he just called a thief without witnesses. So this case teaches nothing about רבי זירא's question.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what are we dealing with? It offers a new way to read the case

phrases.english: No, here, what are we dealing with?
For example, where they came before us
while both of them were holding it,
and we said to them: Go split it,
and they left, and then came back
with one of them holding it,
This one says: He admitted to me.
phrases.notes: The one holding it says the other agreed the whole garment was his.

phrases.english: And that one says: I rented it to him for money,
Where we say to him:
Until now you suspected him of being a robber,
and now you rent it to him without witnesses?

steps.triggerLanguage: לא הכא במאי עסקינן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 15 by reading the ברייתא as a different case
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof is rejected. רבי זירא's question is not decided either way.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא does not have to be about a grab in front of the court. It can be about a later, unbelievable rental claim.

steps.title: Holding the edge of the garment counts for nothing
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the ברייתא means what it says. One person holds the garment, and the other only clutches its edge. It teaches that even סומכוס agrees the edge-holder has no share.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say it is as it is taught: they came before us with one of them holding it, and the other was hanging onto its edge. Even according to סומכוס, who says that money in doubt is split without an oath, סומכוס agrees that holding the edge is worth nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to push away רב נחמן's proof. It reads the ברייתא plainly and shows that this reading is not obvious after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said the plain reading was too obvious. Here the גמרא shows it is not: the other person is clutching the edge of the garment. You might think that is enough to split it, especially for סומכוס, who splits doubtful money easily. The ברייתא teaches that clutching the edge counts for nothing, so it says nothing about grabbing in front of the court.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: it introduces a second answer
Hanging onto the edge of the garment
Money whose owner is in doubt

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new proof. It is a second reason to reject רב נחמן's proof, so רבי זירא's question is still open.

phrases.english: And if you want, say it is as it is taught:

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָתוּ לְקַמַּן כִּי תָּפֵיס לַהּ חַד מִינַּיְיהוּ,
phrases.english: where they came before us with one of them holding it,
and the other was hanging onto its edge,
and even according to Sumchus, who says
money that sits in doubt
is split without an oath,

phrases.aramaic: מוֹדֶה סוֹמְכוֹס דְּסִרְכָא לָאו כְּלוּם הִיא.
phrases.english: Sumchus agrees that holding the edge is nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: ואיבעית אימא כדקתני
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second way to reject the proof from step 15, offered in place of step 16
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only רב נחמן's proof is rejected. The question stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The plain reading is not obvious, because the ברייתא teaches that clutching the edge gives no share, even for סומכוס.

steps.title: If the court takes the garment back, making it הקדש does not work
steps.stepSummary: If a grab in front of the court does not work and the court takes the garment back, then making it הקדש does not work either.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that when one grabs it in front of us, we take it out of his hand, then if he made it הקדש, it is not הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The question is still open, so the גמרא now looks at a related case: making the garment הקדש. This step gives the first side, which is clear. The next step asks about the other side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the grab does not give a person ownership of the whole garment, then he cannot make the whole garment הקדש. A person can only make his own property הקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: If you come to say: it sets up one side of an open question
We take it out of his hand
He made it הקדש, giving it to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: If you come to say
that if one grabbed it in front of us
we take it out of his hand,
then if he made it הקדש, it is not הקדש.

steps.triggerLanguage: אם תמצי לומר תקפה אחד בפנינו מוציאין אותה מידו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proofs are rejected, the גמרא builds on רבי זירא's open question with a הקדש case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a grab in front of the court does not work, making the garment הקדש does not work either.

steps.title: What if he made it הקדש without grabbing it?
steps.stepSummary: If a grab in front of the court does work, the גמרא asks what happens when one person makes the garment הקדש without grabbing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that when one grabs it in front of us, we do not take it out of his hand, then if he made it הקדש without grabbing it, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question that builds on the other side of רבי זירא's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If grabbing gives a person power over the garment, maybe making it הקדש also gives him that power, since it is a strong act. Or maybe only actually taking hold of it counts. Steps 20 and 21 lay out these two sides.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not take it out

steps.whatToRemember: רבי זירא's question about grabbing in front of the court was never answered. רב נחמן's proof was rejected in two ways, and the גמרא now asks how this doubt affects making the garment הקדש.

phrases.english: If you come to say
that if one grabbed it in front of us
we do not take it out of his hand,
then if he made it הקדש without grabbing it, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אם תמצי לומר תקפה אחד בפנינו אין מוציאין אותה מידו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the other side of the open question from step 18 and asks about it
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether making the garment הקדש without grabbing it works like a grab, if grabbing in front of the court does work

steps.title: First side: declaring it הקדש counts like grabbing it
steps.stepSummary: Because a declaration to הקדש is as strong as a physical handover to a regular person, maybe the one who declared the garment הקדש counts as if he grabbed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the Master said that a person's declaration to the Most High is like his handing over to an ordinary person, he is like one who grabbed the garment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first side of the question it just asked in step 19. Maybe saying 'this is הקדש' is as strong as grabbing the garment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule: words alone can transfer something to הקדש, while a sale to a regular person needs a physical handover. Since words to הקדש are that powerful, maybe the declaration does the same job as grabbing the garment in front of the court. If so, the הקדש would work.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Master', a respectful way of quoting a known teaching
His declaration to the Most High, meaning giving something to הקדש with words
His handing over to an ordinary person, a physical transfer in a regular deal
He grabbed it, took hold of it by force

phrases.english: Since the Master said:
his declaration to the Most High
phrases.notes: 'The Most High' means הקדש, giving something to the בית המקדש.

phrases.english: is like his handing over to an ordinary person.
So he is like one who grabbed it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּאָמַר מָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the first side of the question asked in step 19.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a declaration of הקדש count like grabbing the garment in front of the court?

steps.title: Second side: he never grabbed it, so it is not in his possession
steps.stepSummary: Maybe the הקדש does not work, because he did not grab the garment, and the פסוק teaches that one can only make הקדש what is in his possession.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or perhaps: now, at any rate, he did not grab it. And it is written, 'And when a man shall sanctify his house to be holy.' Just as his house is in his possession, so too anything he makes holy must be in his possession. This excludes this garment, which is not in his possession.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the other side of the question. Maybe the הקדש fails because he never actually took the garment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Strong words to הקדש still need something that belongs to you. The פסוק compares everything one makes holy to 'his house', which is clearly his. A garment he never grabbed is not yet in his possession, so maybe he cannot make it הקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: Or perhaps, introduces the other side of a question
He will make holy, give to הקדש
In his possession, under his ownership

steps.whatToRemember: The question has two sides: words to הקדש are as strong as grabbing, or you can only make holy what is already yours.

phrases.english: Or perhaps:
now, at any rate, he did not grab it,
and it is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״וְאִישׁ כִּי יַקְדִּישׁ אֶת בֵּיתוֹ קֹדֶשׁ וְגוֹ׳״,
phrases.english: "And when a man shall sanctify his house to be holy, etc."
just as his house is in his possession,
so too anything he makes holy must be in his possession,
to exclude this, which is not in his possession.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹ דִלְמָא: הַשְׁתָּא מִיהָא הָא לָא תַּקְפַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite side of the question from step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the 'in his possession' rule block the הקדש, since he never grabbed the garment?

steps.title: Starting a story to answer the question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to bring a story that may answer the question about הקדש without grabbing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: for there was a certain...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It starts telling a story that may answer the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Come and hear' tells us an attempted answer is coming. The story itself continues on the next amud. Only then will we see which side of the question it supports.

phrases.english: Come and hear: for there was a certain...

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins an attempted answer to the two-sided question in steps 20–21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Not yet given. The story that may answer it begins here and continues later.
